summary: Moses is tending sheep when he sees a bush burning without being consumed. God speaks to him from the bush, identifying himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God tells Moses he has seen the suffering of the Israelites in Egypt and plans to deliver them to a fertile land. God commissions Moses to go to Pharaoh and lead the Israelites out of Egypt, promising to be with him and revealing his name as "I Am That I Am".
setting: The story is set in the wilderness, specifically at Mount Horeb, which is called "the mountain of God" (v. 1). Moses is tending the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, a priest of Midian (v. 1). The wider situation is that the descendants of Jacob, called the children of Israel, are suffering under Egyptian taskmasters in Egypt (vv. 7, 9). Most historians place the Exodus event, if it occurred, in the Late Bronze Age, but the exact date and historical details are debated.

events.what: Moses leads his father-in-law's flock to Mount Horeb, also called the mountain of God.
An angel of the Lord appears to Moses in a flame of fire from a bush that burns but is not consumed.
Moses decides to turn aside to see why the bush is not burning up.
When God sees Moses turn aside, he calls to him from the bush and tells him to remove his shoes because the ground is holy.
God identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and states that he has seen and heard the suffering of the Israelites in Egypt.
God tells Moses that he is sending him to Pharaoh to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
Moses questions his own ability to go to Pharaoh and lead the Israelites.
God promises to be with Moses and gives a sign: the people will serve God on this mountain after leaving Egypt.

Moses asks what name he should give when the Israelites ask who sent him. God reveals his name as "I Am That I Am" and instructs Moses to tell the Israelites "I Am" and "the Lord God of your fathers" sent him.
God instructs Moses to gather the elders of Israel, tell them about the plan to leave Egypt, and then go with them to Pharaoh to request a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to God.

God predicts Pharaoh will not let the people go easily, but will eventually after God performs wonders. God also states the Israelites will gain favor with the Egyptians and leave with silver, gold, and clothing.

readings.view: This chapter is seen as a foundational moment for Moses' prophecy and the beginning of the redemption from slavery. The revelation of God's name (YHWH) is central to understanding God's nature and covenant with Israel.

The burning bush is sometimes interpreted as a prefigurement of Christ or the Holy Spirit, and Moses' call is often viewed as a model for divine commissioning. The "I Am" statement is sometimes connected to Jesus' "I Am" statements in the New Testament.

This approach examines the text for its literary features, sources, and historical context, often discussing the different names for God (Elohim and YHWH) and the potential for multiple literary layers. It also considers the narrative as a theological account rather than a strictly historical one, questioning the historical accuracy of the events as described.

Moses (Musa) is recognized as a prophet, and the burning bush event is understood as a divine revelation where God speaks to Moses and commands him to go to Pharaoh. The Quran describes a similar encounter where God addresses Moses directly.

oftenQuoted.caution: This verse, "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground," is often quoted to signify reverence or respect for a sacred space. In the surrounding text, God commands Moses to do this specifically because God is present and speaking from the burning bush, making that particular spot holy as part of Moses' direct commissioning.

The phrase "I Am That I Am" is often quoted as God's self-definition or name. In the surrounding text, this is God's answer to Moses' question about what name he should tell the Israelites when they ask who sent him, providing divine authority for Moses' mission.

The phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey" is often used to describe a place of abundance or paradise. In the surrounding text, this phrase describes the specific land God promises to bring the Israelites to, which is currently inhabited by several other peoples, as part of God's promise of deliverance and a new home.
